title: The Suspected Wife (Sotah)
lead: Numbers 5:11–31 sets out the Bible's only ordeal: a wife suspected of adultery, with no witness, drinks holy water mixed with dust and written curses, and God gives the verdict. Ancient and modern readers have found in it both a protection for women and a picture of their unequal place.

sections.b: The law covers a case with no evidence (Numbers 5:13): a husband's jealousy against a wife who may be guilty or innocent. The priest gives her water mixed with dust from the tabernacle floor and the ink of a written curse; if guilty, the curse will "cause your thigh to waste away and your belly to swell" (Numbers 5:21–27), if innocent she is cleared and will bear children (Numbers 5:28). The Mishnah tractate Sotah tightened the conditions, and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai ended the rite in the first century (Mishnah Sotah 9:9). The rabbis drew from it that God lets his name be erased to make peace in a home. Modern scholars disagree: some (Milgrom, Frymer-Kensky) see a safeguard that took the case from an angry husband or crowd; others (Bach and other feminist critics) stress the shame and the one-sidedness. The prophets' picture of Israel as an unfaithful wife (Hosea 2; Ezekiel 16) uses the same language of jealousy.
sections.refs: Numbers 5:11–31; Exodus 32:20; Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:13–22; Hosea 2:2–13; Hosea 4:14; Ezekiel 16:38; John 8:3–11
